title: TS SDK: union-mapper codegen + runtime validators for ergonomic streaming and structured output
creator: Aisha Raman
description:
Goal: provide a small, ergonomic pipeline in the TypeScript SDK that generates both compile-time types and lightweight runtime validators for discriminated unions so applications can safely consume structured outputs from models in both streaming and non-streaming modes. This ticket covers the codegen + runtime glue, an opt-in CLI/loader flow, and runtime streaming parsers that emit partially-validated objects as tokens arrive.

Background: Customers want first-class discriminated-union handling for structured output (e.g., tool calls, multi-type responses). Current ad-hoc parsing patterns lead to brittle runtime checks and poor developer ergonomics when streaming. We need a pattern that: 1) emits TS types + Zod schema/JSON Schema artifacts from a single source-of-truth, 2) supplies a minimal runtime validator (tree-shakeable) for safety, 3) supports streaming partial validation and fail-soft behavior with clear developer opt-ins.

Success criteria:
- CLI or build-time codegen can take a compact union descriptor and emit: .d.ts types, a Zod schema, and an equivalent JSON Schema for downstream systems.
- Runtime helper `guardify()` produced by the SDK exposes isOk/isErr + typed narrowing so callers get proper inference in TypeScript.
- Streaming parser supports `onPartial(validatedChunk)` callbacks and recovers on tag-mismatch with configurable leniency.
- Bundle overhead for the minimal runtime validator < 2.5KB gzipped when tree-shaken.
- Integration examples for tool-calling and chat structured responses added to the examples repo.

Proposed approach:
1) Define a compact, source-first union descriptor format used by product teams (YAML/JSON). Example: `{
  "kind": "union",
  "name": "ActionResult",
  "discriminator": "type",
  "variants": [{"name": "Create", "schema": { ... }}, {"name": "Retry", "schema": { ... }}]
}`
2) Codegen step (ts-node CLI or build plugin) emits: TypeScript types (.d.ts), a Zod schema file (zod schema export), and a JSON Schema artifact. Codegen will also optionally emit a thin `guardify` wrapper that exposes `is<ActionName>` helpers.
3) Runtime: implement a tiny `createValidator` factory that accepts the compiled Zod schema (or JSON Schema via a light runtime adapter) and returns: `validate(obj) => {ok: boolean, errors?: string[]}` plus type guards for narrowing. The runtime adapter will be authored to avoid pulling full Zod at runtime unless requested; by default we ship a micro-validator backed by a custom generated guard when codegen is used.
4) Streaming ergonomics: build a `StreamingUnionParser` that can consume text/stream tokens and attempt incremental parse/validate using the discriminator as soon as present. It exposes events: `onTentative(typedPartial)`, `onValidated(typedObject)`, `onRecoverableError(meta)`, `onFatalError(err)`. Developer can configure `lenient` | `strict` modes.
5) Backwards-compatible opt-in: keep current runtime path (no codegen) working with `lenientParser` that falls back to structural checks. Codegen users get the smaller, faster generated guards.

Design trade-offs considered:
- Full Zod at runtime: pros = feature-complete validation; cons = bundle size and performance. We choose generated guards by default to hit bundle/perf goals and provide an opt-in flag to include Zod if users need complex validation rules.
- Codegen vs runtime reflection: codegen provides best perf and type-safety; runtime reflection keeps DX but will be heavier. We provide both paths but recommend codegen for production workloads.
- Streaming partial-validation complexity: aggressive validation early can increase false negatives if model emits out-of-order tokens. We use discriminator-first heuristics and provide `tolerance` options.

Migration / API examples (TypeScript):
```ts
// generated types (codegen output)
export type ActionResult = { type: 'Create', id: string } | { type: 'Retry', reason: string }

// generated guards (small runtime)
import { isActionResult } from 'generated/guards';

const parsed = await sdk.parseStructured(output, { validator: isActionResult });
if (isActionResult(parsed)) {
  // TS narrows types here
}

// streaming usage
const stream = sdk.streamStructured(prompt, { union: 'ActionResult', mode: 'lenient' });
stream.on('partial', (maybeObj) => { /* receives partially-validated object */ });
stream.on('validated', (obj) => { /* fully validated, typed */ });
```

Acceptance criteria / QA:
- Unit tests for codegen -> types, zod, jsonschema for 6 union shapes (nested, arrays, optional fields).
- Integration test that compares generated guard vs full zod validator on a fuzzed set of model outputs.
- Perf test measuring validator time per object and bundle impact with rollup/esbuild.
- Add one example PR to examples repo demonstrating migrating an existing tool-calling flow to use generated guards and streaming parser.

Implementation plan / tasks:
- [ENG] Implement compact union descriptor parser + codegen (Diego)
- [ENG] Implement minimal generated guard runtime and tree-shaking checks (Samira)
- [ENG] Implement StreamingUnionParser with event hooks + leniency options (Diego)
- [PM] Add example to examples repo and update docs (Ravi)
- [DES] Add small UX copy for lenient/strict modes in SDK docs (Maya)
- [ENG] Perf benchmarks and CI checks (Samira)

Rollout plan:
- Feature gated behind `tsdk.experimental.union_codegen` config.
- Beta: enable for internal Redwood examples + selected customers.
- Gradual enablement and feedback loop for edge-cases (date parsing, multi-token discriminator emission).

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: model outputs that omit discriminator or emit it late -> mitigated by lenient mode and heuristic buffer that waits for discriminator up to N tokens.
- Risk: generated guards missing subtle validation rules -> include optional zod fallback and run fuzzing integration tests pre-release.
- Risk: customers expect seamless runtime semantics change -> strong docs + migration guide + opt-out flag.
